title: Detect Evil Twin Wi-Fi Access Points on Network Devices
shortTitle: Detect Evil Twin Wi-Fi Access Points on Network Devices
summary: This strategy detects evil twin access points, where an adversary stands up a wireless access point that copies the name of a legitimate network so that clients associate with it and expose their traffic. Detection lives in the wireless control plane: wireless controller and access point logs reporting a neighbouring basic service set identifier with a matching service set identifier but a different radio hardware address, sudden client disconnects followed by reassociation to an unknown access point, duplicate service set identifier alerts from the wireless intrusion detection system, and certificate or captive portal failures that show clients rejecting a spoofed network. The pattern is a same name, different hardware address combination on the same channel area. It fails when the wireless controller does not forward rogue access point events, when the site survey is stale, and when the same network name is legitimately broadcast by guest or partner infrastructure.

beginner.definition: An evil twin is a fake wireless network that uses the same name as a real one. People connect to it because it looks familiar. This detection compares what the wireless system sees with the list of approved access points. It catches the fake one by its different hardware address.
beginner.whyItMatters: When a user joins the fake network, their traffic can be read or changed without any warning. The fake access point is often stronger than the real one, so devices choose it. Because the name is identical, users have no reason to suspect anything. Finding it quickly is the only way to protect credentials typed during that session.
howItWorks: Collect wireless controller and access point logs that report nearby and rogue access points.
Collect wireless intrusion detection alerts for duplicate network names in the same area.
Compare every reported network name against the approved access point inventory with its hardware address.
Correlate a wave of client disconnects with immediate reassociation to an unknown access point.
Check whether clients received certificate errors or portal warnings at the same time.
Alert with the physical location, the spoofed name, and the unapproved hardware address.
beginner.example: Think of a sign in sheet at a conference desk. A person writes a name that is already on the list. The name looks right, but the handwriting and the badge number are new. The organiser checks the badge, not the name. The hardware address is that badge.
takeaways: The network name proves nothing; the hardware address of the access point is what you verify.
A burst of disconnects followed by reassociation to an unknown device is a strong combined signal.
A current inventory of approved access points is the foundation of this detection.

objectives: Explain how an evil twin access point tricks a wireless client.
Identify the wireless controller and intrusion detection telemetry that reports rogue access points.
Build a comparison between observed access points and the approved hardware inventory.
Correlate client disconnect waves with reassociation to an unknown access point.
Describe the containment options available on your wireless platform and their limits.
dataSources: Wireless controller logs reporting neighbouring access points with service set identifier, hardware address and signal strength
Wireless intrusion detection system alerts for duplicate service set identifier and spoofed access point detection
Wireless client association and disassociation events including the access point hardware address and the client identity
Network authentication server logs showing repeated failed authentications from clients that just moved networks
Physical site survey records listing approved access point hardware addresses and their installed locations
logic: The pattern is a wireless network name that matches an approved network but is advertised by a hardware address that is not in the approved inventory, especially when it appears in the same physical area and clients move to it quickly. Telemetry shows controller reports of neighbouring access points, intrusion detection duplicate name alerts, and client association records. The fields to correlate are the service set identifier, the access point hardware address, the signal strength or reported location, and the association timestamps of affected clients. What separates malicious from benign is inventory and ownership: a guest or partner access point that is documented and separated from the corporate network is expected, while an undocumented device using a corporate name and drawing clients away from approved access points is not.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Rogue Access Point Advertising an Approved Network Name
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: 'rogue_ap_detected'
#     ssid|in: 'corporate-ssid-list'
#   filter_approved:
#     ap_mac|in: 'approved-ap-inventory'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: high
falsePositives: Guest or partner access points that are permitted to broadcast a similar name in a neighbouring building
A cellular hotspot or a personal router that a staff member brings in and names after the company network
Temporary access points deployed for an event that were not yet added to the approved inventory
tuningNotes: Keep the approved access point inventory current by synchronising it automatically from the wireless controller, because a stale list produces a constant stream of false rogue reports. Filter documented guest and partner networks by hardware address range, and require the reported signal strength to exceed a floor so that distant sightings are ignored. Narrowing by signal strength and by site costs you a low power attacker in a far corner of the building, so keep a weekly report of all unapproved sightings for trend review even when the alert does not fire.
